notes: Independent judgement: unclear. Table 1 content, the '24 individuals resident in the community at the time of the invitation to study' (pp. 7-8) and 'demonstrated higher median scores' (p. 4) are all verified. No characteristics of the consenting group are tabulated. Factual overstatement: 'The only indications are' is not correct. The paper also reports qualitative interviews with 10 participants resident in high or medium security, 10 in low or open wards and 10 in the community at 20 year follow-up (pp. 8, 11), that half of the 10 community interviewees lived in supported accommodation or had a support package and 80 per cent had a baseline primary diagnosis of schizophrenia (p. 8), and keyworker data for 59.1 per cent of living Scottish-based cohort members (p. 6). Corrected wording: replace 'The only indications are' with 'Partial indications are' and add these items. Locator addition: the forensic pathway description is in the Introduction, p. 2.

source_locator: Table 1, p. 3; Methods, Sample, pp. 3-4; Methods, Procedures, p. 4; Limitations, p. 17
notes: Independent judgement: no. Table 1 verified: deceased 89 (36.9) to 31 December 2017; approved 87; no capacity or too unwell 37; outside Scotland 21; no gatekeeper 4; lost 4; total 242 with one person double counted; non-deceased categories sum to 153. Recomputed 56/152 = 36.8, 56/153 = 36.6, 66/153 = 43.1 per cent; against the 241 entered, 56 is 23.2 per cent. The baseline-difference quotation is verbatim (p. 4), as is 'were excluded from the analysis', which in the paper refers to the baseline comparison. Caveats, not errors: deaths are counted to 2017 whereas case note review ran to December 2014, so survivors at assessment numbered at least 152; the paper does not say whether deceased members with notes sit in the group that 'contributed data'. The 56 rests on the author reply only. bias_direction underestimate is defensible because the observed proportion is zero and those too unwell are unlikely to add employed cases.

source_locator: Results, Functional recovery, p. 8; Methods, Data collection, p. 4; Discussion, Functional recovery, p. 14; Conclusion, p. 17; Limitations, p. 17
notes: Independent judgement: unclear, matching both calibration rows. The employment sentence is quoted verbatim (p. 8) and 'no reviewed individuals in paid employment' is on p. 14. The paper gives no definition, reference period, instrument or source for the employment item and defers tools to Appendices A to E and reference 18 (p. 4). Unsupported statement: 'The Feighner diagnostic criteria establish cohort eligibility'. The word Feighner does not appear anywhere in this paper, no diagnostic criteria are named, and cohort eligibility was detention in the State Hospital in 1992/93, not a diagnosis. Corrected final sentence: 'The baseline primary diagnoses in Table 1 describe the cohort, and eligibility was detention in the State Hospital; neither establishes the validity of the employment condition.' Additional support available: the Conclusion refers to failure to 'secure open employment' (p. 17).

notes: Independent judgement: unclear. Table 1 gives interview plus case note review 48/66 and case note review only 18/66 (the printed 72.3 per cent for 48/66 is the paper's own slip; 48/66 is 72.7). Both quotations are verbatim ('a small number of volumes were not available for all living participants', p. 17; 'a single researcher conducted the study introduction, sought informed consent, and collected all data', p. 4). The 16 deceased come from the author reply and are not verifiable in the paper. Omission, not error: the Limitations also state that functional recovery data 'were sourced from ward/community keyworkers only' (p. 17); whether this covers the employment item, which is reported under Functional recovery, is not stated, and it reinforces unclear. Unclear rather than no is appropriate because, unlike Xu 2020, proxy-only ascertainment is not established.

notes: Independent judgement: unclear, with no as a defensible alternative because the paper reports neither numerator, denominator nor interval for the outcome, less than either calibration study. Unclear is retained because the convention directs the item to the suitability of the analysis and a simple proportion suits it. Arithmetic verified: 8/72 = 11.1 per cent; no integer count of 56 or of 66 rounds to 11.1 per cent. Overstatement to note: 'corroborates' is too strong, since 6/54 and 7/63 also give 11.1 per cent; 'is consistent with' is the supportable wording. The 72 = 56 + 16 base is from the author reply and cannot be verified in the paper; the 66 versus 56 discrepancy is real and unreconciled. No adjustment for selective participation is reported. Locators accurate.

notes: Independent judgement: no. Table 1 prints 'Overall participation rate 66/87 (75.9)' and the text confirms it is among those approved by gatekeepers and invited (p. 3). Recomputed 66/153 = 43.1 and 56/152 = 36.8 per cent. The 21 invited non-consenters are derived (87 minus 66), not printed; 21 + 37 + 21 + 8 = 87 = 153 minus 66, so the breakdown is internally consistent. The baseline comparison and the exclusion of those outside Scotland from it are as described (p. 4); no weighting, bounds or sensitivity analysis appears anywhere. Stricter than the Bhullar 2018 calibration row (unclear at about half) and in line with Xu 2020 (no at 53 per cent); the lower rate and the demonstrated baseline differences support no. bias_direction underestimate is defensible given a zero numerator. Locators accurate.
